speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The crime of Sedition has its origins in English common law.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was originally designed to protect the monarchy and the British government from civil unrest and dissent among its people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sedition laws were first introduced in Singapore through the Sedition Ordinance 1938, when Singapore was a British colony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Sedition Act, in its current form, has its roots in the Sedition Ordinance 1948, which was introduced by the British to the Federation of Malaya in 1948 in part to curb local opposition to British colonial rule.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those tendencies are defined in section 3 of the Act including: (a) bringing into hatred or contempt or exciting disaffection against the Government; (b) exciting citizens or residents to attempt to change in unlawful ways, any matter legally established; (c) bringing into hatred or contempt or the exciting of disaffection against the administration of justice in Singapore; (d) raising discontent or disaffection amongst the citizens of Singapore or residents in Singapore; and (e) promoting feelings of ill-will and hostility between different races or classes of the population in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of the key aspects of the Sedition Act are no longer relevant and have not been relevant for a long time.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those provisions have not been used for prosecution.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those provisions which remained in the law up to today, have not been used for a long time.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For instance, the excitement of disaffection against the Government should not be criminalised.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think if it is, a lot of people including many in this House, would be considered criminals.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It had not been done away sooner because some of the other provisions were relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, racial and religious lines are already covered but other classes of the population are not covered.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will, therefore, be making related amendments as we repeal the Sedition Act.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will be making related amendments to the Penal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code to ensure that that aspect to safeguard social cohesion in Singapore is maintained.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We now have laws that deal with conduct that threatens racial and religious harmony, as I had said.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They include sections 298 and 298A of the Penal Code as well as, of course, the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Beyond racial and religious harmony, we must also continue to safeguard social cohesion between other groups of the population.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They could be organised along lines of language, socio-economic status and other groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Section 267C today only covers the use of documents or electronic records.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will be amended to cover speeches and other forms of communication, because they are equally relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill raises the threshold of section 267C by requiring proof of a mental fault element.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The person must have intended for the violence or disobedience to the law or breach of the peace to occur, or knew or had reason to believe that these were likely to occur as a result of his words or actions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Compared to section 3(1)(e) of the Sedition Act, the offence threshold for the amended section 267C will be higher.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill also amends section 267C to define the phrase "counselling disobedience to the law" as providing instruction, advice or information that promotes disobedience to the law.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The amendment is intended to provide greater clarity on the scope of the offence and its application.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Next, I will touch on the amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The offences currently under the Sedition Act are arrestable.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Section 298 of the Penal Code, which criminalises the deliberate wounding of any person's racial or religious feelings.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Section 298A of the Penal Code, which criminalises the promotion of disharmony between different racial or religious feelings.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Section 505 of the Penal Code, which criminalises, among other behaviour, the making, publication or circulation of material with the intent to incite any group of persons to commit an offence against another group of persons.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It said that it had used the Sedition Act in the past to address various forms of conduct that weaken our social fabric and undermine our institutions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, new laws were introduced to deal with these concerns in a more "targeted and calibrated manner", such as the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act (MRHA), Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA), Administration of Justice Act, Undesirable Publications Act, Newspaper and Printing Presses Act (NPPA) and specific provisions under the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But as a result, various provisions in other Acts are being amended.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This plays a useful role of helping to reduce the risk of a suspect being investigated too long after the event and relevant evidence may not be fully available.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With the consequential amendment to section 267C of the Penal Code, this time limit for prosecution would not seem to apply anymore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Should not the time limit for prosecution provision have also been added as an amendment to the Penal Code in this Bill in the same way that this Bill makes the offences described in sections 298, 298A and 505 of the Penal Code arrestable, because they are arrestable in the now to be repealed Sedition Act?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My concern here is with the phrase "information that promotes disobedience to the law and such order".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, a lecturer may teach a module on the history of civil disobedience as part of a course in history or politics or citizens may convey information to one another on social media about acts of civil disobedience that have been committed elsewhere or in the past or ideas relating to the philosophical arguments for and/or against civil disobedience.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If there is no specific intent to induce a person to commit a specific act of civil disobedience in Singapore that can be demonstrated from the said sharing of information, would this still constitute an offence?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think it should not but I welcome the Minister's assurance on this point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My third point, Madam, is that this Bill makes offences under 298 and 298A arrestable, which the Minister just alluded to, meaning that the Police may arrest without a warrant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No doubt these powers were already in the now to be repealed Sedition Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, I would like to ask for clarification about why these offences are now being made arrestable in the Penal Code for the following reasons.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Hence, MHA proposes to make, among other things, sections 298 and 298A in the Penal Code that deal with conduct that threatens social cohesion and harmony arrestable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The problem is, sections 298 and 298A are broadly worded.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Section 3(1) of the now to be repealed Sedition Act defines a seditious tendency and includes in section 3(1)(e) "to promote feelings of ill-will and hostility between different races or classes of the population of Singapore." Critically, however, section 3(2) of the now to be repealed Sedition Act sets out a list of exceptions to specify what shall not be deemed as seditious and I quote from this section 3(2) of the now to be repealed Sedition Act, "Notwithstanding subsection (1), any act, speech, words, publication or other thing shall not be deemed to be seditious by reason only that it has a tendency: (a) to show that the Government has been misled or mistaken in any of its measures; (b)	to point out errors or defects in the Government or the Constitution as by law established or in legislation or in the administration of justice with a view to the remedying of such errors or defects; (c)	to persuade the citizens of Singapore or the residents in Singapore to attempt to procure by lawful means the alteration of any matter in Singapore; or (d)	to point out, with a view to their removal, any matters producing or having a tendency to produce feelings of ill-will and enmity between different races or classes of the population of Singapore, if such act, speech, words, publication or other thing has not otherwise in fact a seditious tendency." Section 4 then sets out the list of offences under the Sedition Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps the safeguards come in the requirement that there must be "deliberate intention" to wound the religious or racial feelings of any person in section 298.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In section 298A, the offender must know that they are promoting or attempting to promote feelings of ill will and so on between different racial or religious groups or must know that they are committing an act which is prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between different religious or racial groups in which disturbs or is likely to disturb public tranquility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, I am not sure if such requirements in section 298 and 298A of the Penal Code really provide for the same safeguards as section 3(2) of the Sedition Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In particular, I am concerned about the scope of the new section 298A(b).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, will the Police investigate such conduct as a potential offence?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, is there a threshold for what constitutes egregious and if so, what are some of the criteria for it?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Determining such offences involves judgement and by making these offences arrestable and giving the Police the power to arrest without a warrant, would that not increase the risk of the wrong judgement being made, which might potentially inflame a delicate situation further?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How would that risk be mitigated and managed?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Statutes Online facility does not reflect any MRHA amendment being enforced from 2019.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The last amendment reflected there is in 2011.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I wanted to say I thank Members for the overwhelming support for this Bill to repeal the Sedition Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fact that only Mr Perera wanted to speak, I think, does suggest overwhelming support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he supports it as well, so, I thank him for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will address the clarifications that Mr Perera has raised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the first question that he asked is the time limit for prosecution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To understand this, I think we need to look at the Sedition Act a little carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The six-month time limit is in section 5 of the Sedition Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 5, then, must relate back to section 4, for example, 4(1)(a), where any person who does or attempts to do or makes any preparation to do anything which would have a seditious tendency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That, in turn, brings you back to section 3(1), which defines what seditious tendency is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A seditious tendency is a tendency to bring into hatred or contempt or to excite disaffection against the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at (d), "to raise discontent or disaffection amongst the citizens of Singapore or the residents in Singapore"; (e), "to promote feelings of ill-will and hostility between different races or classes of the population of Singapore".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you went out there and you said something that makes people upset with the Government of Singapore, under section 3(1)(a), that is an offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, I think on the strict wordings of section 3, Mr Leon Perera would have committed offences several times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am likely to have committed offences several times as well, both in my previous incarnation and now, because it talks about raising discontent, disaffection amongst the citizens of Singapore and exciting disaffection against the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These all really have not been relevant for a very long time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over a period of time, different provisions come up, as I explained in my Second Reading opening speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, the Administration of Justice Act on contempt of Court, on interfering with proceedings in Court, on bringing that disrepute to the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is legislation that deals with that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 267C takes some parts of section 4.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is really on violence, getting people to violently do something and contrary to the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no complete taking of the Sedition Act and putting it in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What you now have with the other pieces of legislation are completely different animals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The essence or the heart of the Sedition Act is actually being done away with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the rationale for the six months has got to be seen in the context of what the Sedition Act provides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the other legislation, in normal criminal cases, you take the normal criminal approach, which is that there is no time limit on prosecuting offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, for example, if you look at section 267C, which is the amendment that is coming along, section 267C of the Penal Code is an existing provision with no time limits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It originally dealt with usage, making, printing, reproducing, distributing, communicating any incitement to violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you can see it is a very different type of offence, counselling disobedience to the law or to lawful order of a public servant, which is likely to lead to a breach of the peace.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got nothing to do with exciting disaffection against the Government or making people unhappy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a very direct focused offence and we are making some changes there, including to the mental elements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Bits and pieces which are relevant for modern Singapore have already been moved out into other legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, one last bit is being moved out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point that Mr Perera makes on the counselling of civil disobedience and the mental element.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, if you look at section 267C, conveying information about civil disobedience is, in and of itself, not an offence under section 267C because if you look at section 267C, it has got (1)(a), (b), (c), (d), then it says, in the proposed amendments, the person does any of these things, intending for violence, disobedience to the law or such lawful order or breach of the peace to occur.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the person must have intended for the violence or the disobedience or the breach of the peace to occur, or knowing, or having reason to believe, that such consequences would occur.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third point Mr Perera makes is why is it being made arrestable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I think you need to compare sections 298 to 298A, which are already in our Statute books, with section 3(1).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I just took the House through section 3(1).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I mentioned, a large number of us would probably have run afoul of section 3(1) at one point of time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have got to look at section 3(1) and you have got to see what is important is that section 3(1)(a), "A seditious tendency is a tendency to bring into hatred or contempt or excite disaffection against the Government".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, of course, you have got (b), (c), (d), (e), some of which have been moved over in the past and one aspect is being moved over now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, section 3(2) says it shall not be deemed to be seditious by reason only that you are trying to show that the Government has been misled or mistaken; or you are pointing out errors or defects in the Government as by law established; or you are trying to persuade citizens of Singapore, the residents in Singapore to attempt to procure by lawful means the alteration of any matter in Singapore; or to point out, with a view to their removal, any matters producing or having a tendency to produce feelings of ill-will and enmity between different races or classes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you see this is really nothing to do with the offences that are now found in other legislation, including the slight amendments to section 267C which is on counselling disobedience to the law or the view to breaking of the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Sedition Act section 3(2)(d) has some reference to producing feelings of ill-will and enmity between different races or classes, but you must look at it in the light also of section 3(3), which says the intention of the person charged at the time he did some of these things, seditious words are irrelevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you did what you did and it has these tendencies, then you are liable under the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is a very different animal, very different kind of offence and one could almost say very sui generis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at sections 298 and 298A, which, by the way, is not an issue today, "whoever by words, spoken or written, or by signs or visible representation, promote or attempts to promote, on the grounds of religion or race, ill-will and commits any act which he knows is prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between different religious groups".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the element of intention is incorporated in section 298A(b).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is relevant today insofar as offences are being made arrestable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, one can ask: does it have to be made arrestable?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think the question can be asked by reference to the Sedition Act which, as I have said, deals with quite different subjects and the exceptions do not make sense in the context of these provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think it is legitimate to ask.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Perera's fourth and final point is whether the MRHA amendments are already in force.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we answered a Parliamentary Question in September.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You cannot just bring the Act into force without making sure – religious organisations are differently resourced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some are essentially a very small operation – to give time to all of them to resource themselves, to be able to comply with the requirements of the legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, you have got to take time to educate them, talk to them about the requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also have to make sure that our own systems are set up to be able to receive the information that comes through.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another subject which I have spoken about quite frequently in this House is that we are short of officers and we now have to find officers who can be trained to deal with these specific returns that the religious groups will be giving.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there are a number of different factors here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will do this as quickly as we can.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said the training of the Investigation Officers on the thresholds for the amended offences is ongoing and that will take a little bit of time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, on the ground, as in the religious organisations, also need a little bit of time.
